subject: English

intro: Lesson 50: Non-fiction: whose stories get told?. Read the whole text, then answer the questions. Annotate methods and their effects in the margin.

passage.title: The Nurse History Forgot
paras: Ask most people to name a nurse from the Crimean War and they will say Florence Nightingale. Fewer will name Mary Seacole, yet her story is just as remarkable.

Mary Seacole was born in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805. Her mother ran a boarding house and was a respected healer, and Mary learned from her how to care for the sick using herbal remedies. As a young woman she travelled widely, and in Panama she treated people during an outbreak of cholera.

When the Crimean War began in 1853, British soldiers were dying in great numbers, more from disease than from battle. In 1854 Seacole travelled to London and offered to join the nurses being sent to the war. Her offer was turned down. She did not give up. She travelled to Crimea at her own expense and, near Balaclava, opened the 'British Hotel', a place where sick and tired soldiers could find food, comfort and care. She often rode out to the battlefield itself to help the wounded.

After the war, Seacole returned to London poor, but the soldiers had not forgotten her: a festival was held in her honour in 1857, and in the same year she published her life story, Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands. Then, for most of the next century, history largely forgot her.

Today she is remembered again. In 2004 she was voted the greatest Black Briton, and in 2016 a statue of her was unveiled outside St Thomas' Hospital in London. Her story asks a question that every history book should ask: whose stories have we left out?
